entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Apollo Theater in Harlem, New York City is the most important venue in the history of African American music and entertainment, transformed from a whites-only burlesque house to Black performance venue in 1934. The Apollo's Amateur Night — still held on Wednesdays — launched the careers of Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan, Billie Holiday, James Brown, Stevie Wonder, Marvin Gaye, Jimi Hendrix, Michael Jackson, and Luther Vandross, establishing the Apollo as the crucible of American popular music.

Frank Schiffman and Leo Brecher purchased the 125th Street theater in 1934 and immediately opened it to Black performers and audiences, breaking Harlem's racial entertainment barrier at the height of the Harlem Renaissance. The Amateur Night tradition, where audiences judged acts (and booed off poor performers), became the defining test of raw talent. Ella Fitzgerald won in 1934, launching a career that redefined jazz singing. James Brown recorded 'Live at the Apollo' (1963), which became the best-selling live album in history at the time.

The Apollo was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1983 and became a non-profit in 1991. The theater's symbolic importance in Black American culture equals its musical importance: during the Civil Rights movement, the Apollo hosted fundraisers; after Martin Luther King's assassination, his body lay in repose at the Apollo as 150,000 mourners filed past. Today the Apollo hosts the Tony Goldwyn-led Apollo Theater Foundation and its education programs reaching 350,000+ students annually.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Apollo Theater's Amateur Night launched the careers of virtually every major Black American musical artist from Ella Fitzgerald to Michael Jackson, making it the single most important incubator of American popular music.
